1	# SmolVLM: Redefining Small and Efficient Multimodal Models
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05299
     5	
     6	## Overview
     7	
     8	SmolVLM is a family of compact vision-language models (VLMs) from Hugging Face and Stanford University, designed for resource-efficient inference on mobile and edge devices. The series includes three model sizes — 256M, 500M, and 2.2B parameters — that achieve competitive performance against much larger models while using dramatically less GPU memory. The smallest model, SmolVLM-256M, runs inference with less than 1GB GPU RAM and outperforms the 300× larger Idefics-80B model. All weights, datasets, code, and a mobile app (HuggingSnap) are fully open-sourced.
     9	
    10	## Architecture Design
    11	
    12	![SmolVLM Architecture](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    13	
    14	SmolVLM uses a pipeline where images are split into sub-images, encoded by a SigLIP vision encoder, compressed via pixel shuffle (space-to-depth), projected through a linear layer into the SmolLM2 language model's input space, and concatenated with text token embeddings. For video, frames are sampled and processed similarly.
    15	
    16	Three critical architectural findings drive the design:
    17	
    18	**Finding 1 — Balanced Encoder-LM Compute:** Compact VLMs benefit from smaller vision encoders. A 93M SigLIP-B/16 paired with a 135M LM outperforms a 428M SigLIP-SO400M with the same LM. Only at 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead.
    19	
    20	**Finding 2 — Extended Context Length:** Performance improves significantly when extending context from 2K to 16K tokens. This was achieved by increasing the RoPE base from 10K to 273K and fine-tuning on mixed long/short-context data. The 2.2B model uses 16K context; smaller variants use 8K.
    21	
    22	**Finding 3 — Aggressive Token Compression:** Pixel shuffle rearranges spatial features into channels, reducing visual tokens by r². While larger models use r=2, small VLMs benefit from r=4 (16× token reduction), easing attention overhead and improving long-context modeling.
    23	
    24	![Pixel Shuffle Diagram](./assets/figure_6.jpg)
    25	
    26	## Benchmark Performance
    27	
    28	SmolVLM was evaluated across 13 benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. The "Efficient OS" column shows the best open-source model under similar constraints.
    29	
    30	| Capability | Benchmark | SmolVLM 256M | SmolVLM 500M | SmolVLM 2.2B | Best Efficient OS |
    31	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    32	| Single-Image | OCRBench | 52.6% | 61.0% | 72.9% | 54.7% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    33	| Single-Image | AI2D | 46.4% | 59.2% | 70.0% | 71.0% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    34	| Single-Image | ChartQA | 55.6% | 62.8% | 68.7% | 48.0% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    35	| Single-Image | TextVQA | 50.2% | 60.2% | 73.0% | 61.5% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    36	| Single-Image | DocVQA | 58.3% | 70.5% | 80.0% | 77.7% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    37	| Single-Image | ScienceQA | 73.8% | 80.0% | 89.6% | 87.5% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    38	| Multi-task | MMMU | 29.0% | 33.7% | 42.0% | 33.9% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    39	| Multi-task | MathVista | 35.9% | 40.1% | 51.5% | 37.6% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    40	| Multi-task | MMStar | 34.6% | 38.3% | 46.0% | 43.1% (Molmo-A1B-7B) |
    41	| Video | Video-MME | 33.7% | 42.2% | 52.1% | 45.0% (InternVL2-2B) |
    42	| Video | MLVU | 40.6% | 47.3% | 55.2% | 48.2% (InternVL2-2B) |
    43	| **Average** | **All Benchmarks** | **44.0%** | **51.0%** | **59.8%** | — |
    44	
    45	**RAM Usage:** SmolVLM-256M uses 0.8 GB (batch=1), SmolVLM-500M uses 1.2 GB, and SmolVLM-2.2B uses 4.9 GB. For comparison, Molmo-A1B-7B requires 27.7 GB.
    46	
    47	## On-Device Deployment
    48	
    49	![Mobile App and Throughput](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    50	
    51	SmolVLM runs on-device via the HuggingSnap iOS app, processing photos and videos entirely locally with no cloud dependency. Throughput benchmarks across Apple Silicon devices show:
    52	
    53	- SmolVLM-256M achieves up to ~80 tokens/second on Pro M1 Max 64GB
    54	- At batch size 64, the 256M model reaches nearly 1000 tokens/second on high-end devices
    55	- Even on a MacBook Air M3 16GB, the 256M model produces ~55 tokens/second
    56	- Throughput scales roughly linearly with batch size for the smallest model
    57	
    58	## Key Findings
    59	
    60	- **Sub-1GB inference is achievable:** SmolVLM-256M uses only 0.8 GB GPU RAM at batch size 1, enabling deployment on smartphones and low-power edge devices.
    61	- **SmolVLM-256M surpasses the 300× larger Idefics-80B** despite an 18-month development gap, demonstrating that architectural efficiency matters more than raw scale.
    62	- **Balanced encoder-LM sizing, aggressive pixel shuffle (r=4), and extended context (up to 16K tokens)** are the three most impactful design choices for compact VLMs.
    63	- **SmolVLM-2.2B rivals state-of-the-art models** that consume twice the GPU memory, achieving 59.8% average across 13 benchmarks.
    64	- **All models, data, code, and a mobile app are fully open-sourced** to promote reproducibility and on-device AI research.

    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml

# Create 16:9 presentation
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Define a dark, technical color palette
DARK_BG = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x1A, 0x2E)       # near-black navy
ACCENT = RgbColor(0x00, 0xC8, 0xFF)        # cyan accent
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
LIGHT_GRAY = RgbColor(0xCC, 0xCC, 0xCC)
MEDIUM_GRAY = RgbColor(0x88, 0x88, 0x88)
HIGHLIGHT = RgbColor(0xFF, 0x6B, 0x35)     # orange highlight

def add_background(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color

def add_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size, font_color, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name='Calibri'):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.color.rgb = font_color
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = align
    return txBox

def add_bullet_text(slide, left, top, width, height, bullets, font_size, font_color, font_name='Calibri'):
    txBox = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = txBox.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    for i, bullet in enumerate(bullets):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = bullet
        p.font.size = font_size
        p.font.color.rgb = font_color
        p.font.name = font_name
        p.level = 0
        p.space_after = Pt(10)
    return txBox

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 1: Title Slide
# ============================================================
blank_layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # blank
slide1 = prs.slides.add_slide(blank_layout)
add_background(slide1, DARK_BG)

# Accent bar at top
shape = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.15))
shape.fill.solid()
shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT
shape.line.fill.background()

# Title
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(0.8), Inches(2.2), Inches(11.7), Inches(1.2),
            'SmolVLM: Redefining Small and Efficient Multimodal Models',
            Pt(44), WHITE, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')

# Subtitle / authors
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(0.8), Inches(3.5), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.6),
            'Hugging Face & Stanford University',
            Pt(22), LIGHT_GRAY, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')

# One-liner
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(1.5), Inches(4.3), Inches(10.3), Inches(0.8),
            'Compact VLMs that achieve competitive performance with dramatically lower memory footprints through strategic architectural optimizations.',
            Pt(18), MEDIUM_GRAY, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')

# Key stat badge
shape = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, Inches(4.5), Inches(5.4), Inches(4.3), Inches(0.7))
shape.fill.solid()
shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = RgbColor(0x2A, 0x2A, 0x4E)
shape.line.color.rgb = ACCENT
add_textbox(slide1, Inches(4.5), Inches(5.55), Inches(4.3), Inches(0.5),
            'Sub-1GB Inference | 256M / 500M / 2.2B Parameters',
            Pt(16), ACCENT, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 2: Problem / Motivation
# ============================================================
slide2 = prs.slides.add_slide(blank_layout)
add_background(slide2, DARK_BG)

# Accent bar
shape = slide2.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.08))
shape.fill.solid()
shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT
shape.line.fill.background()

add_textbox(slide2, Inches(0.7), Inches(0.5), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
            'Large VLMs Are Powerful but Impractical for Edge Deployment',
            Pt(32), WHITE, bold=True, font_name='Calibri')

bullets = [
    'State-of-the-art VLMs (e.g., Idefics-80B) require tens of gigabytes of GPU memory, making mobile/edge deployment infeasible.',
    'Existing efficient open-source models still consume 10–30 GB RAM, far exceeding smartphone and IoT device limits.',
    'The gap between research-scale models and on-device inference creates a bottleneck for real-world multimodal applications.',
    'Key challenge: achieve competitive vision-language understanding without sacrificing the memory and latency constraints of edge hardware.'
]
add_bullet_text(slide2, Inches(0.7), Inches(1.4), Inches(12), Inches(3.5), bullets, Pt(20), LIGHT_GRAY, font_name='Calibri')

# Comparison stat boxes
box_data = [
    ('Idefics-80B', '80B', '>> 30 GB', HIGHLIGHT),
    ('Molmo-A1B-7B', '7B', '27.7 GB', HIGHLIGHT),
    ('InternVL2-2B', '2B', '~10 GB', HIGHLIGHT),
    ('SmolVLM-256M', '256M', '0.8 GB', RgbColor(0x00, 0xE6, 0x7A))
]
for i, (name, params, ram, color) in enumerate(box_data):
    left = Inches(0.7 + i * 3.1)
    top = Inches(5.0)
    shape = slide2.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, left, top, Inches(2.8), Inches(1.8))
    shape.fill.solid()
    shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = RgbColor(0x2A, 0x2A, 0x4E)
    shape.line.color.rgb = color
    add_textbox(slide2, left, top + Inches(0.15), Inches(2.8), Inches(0.4), name, Pt(16), WHITE, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')
    add_textbox(slide2, left, top + Inches(0.55), Inches(2.8), Inches(0.4), params, Pt(28), color, bold=True, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')
    add_textbox(slide2, left, top + Inches(1.05), Inches(2.8), Inches(0.4), ram, Pt(16), LIGHT_GRAY, bold=False, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER, font_name='Calibri')

# ============================================================
# SLIDE 3: Architecture Overview
# ============================================================
slide3 = prs.slides.add_slide(blank_layout)
add_background(slide3, DARK_BG)

shape = slide3.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(0.08))
shape.fill.solid()
shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT
shape.line.fill.background()

add_textbox(slide3, Inches(0.7), Inches(0.5), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
            'SmolVLM Architecture: Image Splitting, Pixel Shuffle, and SmolLM2 Backbone',
            Pt(32), WHITE, bold=True, font_name='Calibri')

# Add architecture image
img_path = '/app/benchmark/assets/figure_3.jpg'
slide3.shapes.add_picture(img_path, Inches(0.7), Inches(1.3), width=Inches(8.5))

# Pipeline steps on the right
steps = [
    ('1. Image Splitting', 'Input image is divided into sub-images for local processing.'),
    ('2. Vision Encoder', 'SigLIP encoder extracts patch-level visual features.'),
    ('3. Pixel Shuffle', 'Spatial features rearranged into channels (r² token reduction).'),
    ('4. Linear Projection', 'Visual tokens projected into SmolLM2 input embedding space.'),
    ('5. SmolLM2 Backbone', 'Compact language model fuses vision and text for generation.')
]
